components.html:
See the "H" on my carriage? In my frustration when I first got my machine, I took a Sharpie and marked the hold (Russel) levers ...
Maybe seeing my handwritten "H" in this course will help you remember which is which.

One of the many good things about the LK-150 is the fact that there are only 2 sets levers to learn!
  • Russel Levers
  • Side Levers
But you can do SO MUCH with these levers!

components.title: Gain a better understanding of what's happening with the knitting carriage

components.html:
The LK-150 is a manual knitting machine. This means there are no punchards or electronics to "select" and position needles.
Don't let this stop you from exploring stitch patterning on this machine!
Use a cheat sheet to make selecting needles easier

This clever device makes quick work of manually selecting needles.
It is available from Kriskrafter

A tuck is a stitch that is not knitted, but looped over the needle. If we tuck over the same needle for a number of rows, the loops gather on those needles, instead of knitting. This creates raised bundles. When the bundles are gathered and knit, the fabric is distorted from plain knitting, resulting in texture.
The fun comes in various needle arrangements alternating with plain knitting. Tucking while alternating colors and even tucking with needles out of work.
The yarn and the tension play a role in creating beautiful tuck patterns.

Because the LK-150 is a manual machine, we need to pull needles to Hold Position "D" when working in stitch pattern.
TO SELECT NEEDLES:
  • Use needle pushers
  • Mark the needlebed
  • Use a cheat sheet to make selecting the needles easier.

Knitting Charts and Punchcards
Tuck charts for hand manipulated machines often look like this.

LK150 knitters can also use punchcard designs. A tuck punchcard will be mostly holes (black) (see below).
To hand manipulate needles, you will be pulling needles to correspond with the white spaces.

slides.caption:
Beautiful texture with tuck
Use the 1x1 needle pusher | Engage both Russel levers
  • Row 1: Pull every other needle to D position. Knit across, tucking every other needle
  • Row 2: Repeat row 1 (tucking the same needles)
  • Row 3: Pull the opposite needles to D position . Knit across, tucking every other needle
Tuck 440 Punchcard

Combine with color changes for an interesting effect.
Change colors every 6 rows
Tuck Baby Punchcard

Tuck doesn't have to be all-over. Tuck stitches can be grouped to create interesting texture.
Place tuck stitches in diagonal columns
Diagonal Tuck punchcard

Knit tuck as "motifs"
Heart Tuck Punchcard

Exercise #1 - plain knitting
  1. No yarn in the carriage
  2. Pull 20 needles to "D" Position
  3. Carriage Set for Plain Knitting (Both side levers and Russel Levers are dis-engaged)
  4. Push carriage from right to left.  What Happens?
  5. Push carriage from left to right.  What Happens?

Exercise #2 - Hold all Needles
  1. No yarn in the carriage
  2. Pull 20 needles to "D" Position
  3. Carriage Set to HOLD (Both Russel Levers are engaged)
  4. Push carriage from right to left.  What Happens?
  5. Push carriage from left to right.  What Happens?

Exercise #3 - Hold Individual needles - The basis of patterning
  1. No yarn in the carriage
  2. Pull 20 needles to "D" Position
  3. Using the 1x1 needle pusher, push every other needle to "B" (working) position
  4. Set the LEFT Russel Lever to HOLD
  5. Push carriage from right to left.  What Happens?
  6. Push carriage from left to Right  What Happens?
Exercise #4 hold groups of needles - The basis of Partial Knitting and Short Row shaping
  1. No yarn in the carriage
  2. Carriage on the right
  3. Pull 20 needles to "B" (Working) Position
  4. Using the flat edge of the needle pusher, pull 10 needles (on the left) to "D" (hold) position
  5. Set BOTH Russel Levers to HOLD
  6. Push carriage from right to left.  What Happens?
  7. Push carriage from left to right  What Happens?

Cast on 20 stitches with any method, hang some weight and knit a few rows

Exercise #1- plain knitting - Carriage Setting
Part 1: Plain Knitting (stockinette)
  1. All needles in "B" working position
  2. Carriage Set for Plain Knitting (Both side levers and Russel Levers are disengaged)
  3. Knit from Right to Left then Left to Right (plain/normal knitting)
Part 2:
  1. All needles in "B" working position
  2. Carriage on the right, engage the Left Russel lever. Knit to the Left. What happens?  Why?
  3. Knit back to the right

NOTE: To hold needles, the carriage needs to be set to hold AND the needles need to be in "D" Hold position.

Exercise #2 -Needle settings
  1. Carriage Set for Plain Knitting (Both side levers and Russel Levers are dis-engaged)
  2. Pull all the needles to "D" Hold position
  3. Push carriage from Right to Left.  What Happens?
  4. Push carriage from Left to Right  What Happens?
     It takes BOTH the carriage setting and the needle position to tuck.

NOTE: To hold needles, the carriage needs to be set to hold AND the needles need to be in "D" Hold position.

Exercise #3 - Hold all needles - free pass
  1. Carriage on the right Pull ALL needles to "D" Position
  2. Carriage set to "hold" (Both Russel Levers engaged)
  3. Push carriage from Right to Left.  What Happens?
  4. Push carriage from Left to Right.  What Happens?  
    Notice that the working yarn travels across the needles and nothing knits BUT no stitches drop either.
    This can be used for "free pass" to position the carriage   Why free pass?

Exercise #4 hold groups of needles - The basis of partial knitting and short row shaping
  1. Knit 2 rows plain to make sure needles are in working position.
  2. Using the flat edge of the needle pusher, pull 10 needles to "D" (hold) position
  3. Set BOTH Russel Levers to HOLD
  4. Push carriage from Right to Left. What Happens?
  5. Push carriage from Left to Right. What Happens?

Exercise #5 hold individual needles - The basis stitch patterning
  1. Knit a few rows across all needles
  2. Use the 1x1 needle pusher and push every other needle to "D" (hold) position
  3. Set BOTH Russel Levers to HOLD
  4. Push carriage from Right to Left.  What Happens?
  5. Push carriage from Left to Right.  What Happens?
  6. Cancel hold (set for plain knitting  - disengage the Russel Levers)
  7. Knit across all needles
  8. Knit a few rows

The previous exercises were designed to help you UNDERSTAND the concept of putting needle in hold for Free Pass, Partial Knitting, Short Row shaping and Tuck Stitch patterns.
Instead of referring to (or memorizing) the chart in your manual, remember:
There are 2 steps to using "hold"
  • The carriage setting with the Russel Levers | and ||
  • The needle positions "D" position (all the way out)

components.html:
Use even weight to help keep the tuck strands taut enough to knit smoothly.
When establishing your stitch pattern, Check to confirm the tuck stitches knit correctly on the closing row.
As you are knitting, pull the work down now and then.
Even if you have the work weighted properly, the tuck stitches tend to gather up and get caught.
Which side is the right side???
Your choice! That's the beauty of many tuck stitch patterns, they are reversible!
You can't tuck 2 needles side by side
This is true for many automatic patterning machines (punchcard or electronic), but the LK-150 WILL allow you to tuck across 2 stitches. Notice how the tuck travels between the 2 needles. Knit carefully for success.
Having trouble knitting with tuck?
  • Knit fewer tuck rows - less strands = easier knitting
  • Knit the closing row manually. Hand knit each stitch to ensure the tucks knit properly. After manually knitting one row, Cancel hold on the carriage, pull the needles all the way out and carefully knit the next row.

Tuck stitch patterns are wider than stockinette.
They allow you to knit wider pieces, minimizing the needlebed size limitations (total number of needles available).
Tuck stitch patterns are shorter than stockinette.
You'll need to knit more rows for the same length.
Tuck stitch takes more yarn than other stitch patterns
Plan accordingly
When manually tucking on your machine, avoid the end needles.
Do not tuck the end 1-2 needles for easier seaming and a neater edge.

components.html:
Try out this beautiful stitch pattern. (Remember the needles out of work remain out of work throughout the entire sample)
  1. Pull out 39 stitches (or an odd number)
  2. Push every other needle to "A" (out of work position) keeping the edge needles in working position
  3. Cast on over the needles in work (every other needle)
  4. Hang your cast on comb
  5. Knit 2 rows
  6. Hang claw weight
  7. From the needles that are in working position, pull every other needle to hold position
  8. Set the carriage to hold in both directions
  9. Knit 4 rows
  10. Cancel Hold
  11. Knit 1 row (all needles should knit)
  12. Working with the needles in work, pull out the opposite set of every other needles to hold position
  13. Set carriage to hold
  14. Knit 4 rows
  15. Cancel Hold
  16. Knit 1 row
Repeat this sequence 8-10 times. Bind off or drop the swatch from the machine.

Sometimes you just want a LITTLE texture to your knitting. Simple tuck stitches can add bulk (and width).
Here are 3 variations, I'll bet you'll be surprised (as I was) to compare the knit side of these tuck samples)


In this sample, you are tucking every other needle and tucking on every row.  The fabric is quite dense, but look at the interesting columns of knit stitches!


Search "tuck" in the Knit it Now Learning Library, you'll find over 30 tutorials about this versatile technique.


This time, alternate the tucked needles again, but add a plain row of knitting between.  This makes a much less dense fabric, and IMHO (in my humble opinion) the knit side looks best!

For some tuck "eye candy" take a look at tuck in the Knit it Now Stitch Library - imagine all the variations!


Tuck the same needles every other row .... wow!  I can see the knit side of this substituting for ribbing.  There isn't any stretch, but the look would be a great contrast to plain 'ol stockinette or reverse stockinette.

Hand manipulated knit and purl stitches PLUS tuck EQUALS Fisherman rib. This classic stitch pattern is thick, warm, textured, reversible and stretchy.
It's perfect for scarves, earwarmers, hats, fingerless mitts ... whatever you can imagine.
With this technique you can work this on any manual machine, including the LK-150
Although this video is showing a standard gauge machine, it is demonstrating manual needle selection as you would work on your LK-150 machine.
This is is the same tuck pattern in 1 color! Great visual interest and texture!

When your needles are all the way out to "D" position
AND
the Russel Levers are engaged |,
the needles don't knit and nothing happens.

Here are 5 reasons for using this setting


Free Pass


For some reason you need to position your carriage on the opposite side of the bed. Let's say you ripped out a row or two. Your working yarn is on the left side of the bed and the carriage is on the right. Use hold to get the carriage back into position.
  1. Pull all needles to "D" hold
  2. Set the carriage to hold (both Russel Levers engaged | )
  3. FREE PASS to the opposite side of the bed
  4. Reset your row counter

Partial Knitting

You may be knitting a child's sweater and want to put a slit at the back neck opening to make it easier to pull over the head.
Your pattern may tell you to "hold 25 needles left of 0" and continue knitting for 15 rows. You would use hold to knit one side of the back without taking the other side off the needlebed.
  1. Pull 25 needles left of 0 to "D" hold
  2. Set the carriage to hold (Both Russel levers engaged |)
  3. Follow the pattern for one side of the knitting
  4. Bind off as instructed and take those needles out of work
  5. Break the working yarn
  6. Cancel Hold (Both Russel Levers NOT engaged) ||
  7. Re-thread the carriage
  8. Follow the pattern instructions for the remaining side
  9. Bind off as instructed

Short Row Shaping


Short row shaping (also called partial knitting) is use to create curves in your knitting. From bust darts to sock toes and heels, shaping mittens to shaping necklines, short rows are a staple in a machine knitter's bag of tricks. Although outside the scope of this course, Knit it Now has extensive information about using short row shaping.

Stitch Patterning


This is where the fun stuff happens! The possibilities for putting needles in hold to create stitch patterns are practically endless!
Please take time to explore tuck stitch and all its variations.

Super-Fast, Closed Cast On


Not only is this cast on fast AND easy to remember, it provides instant gathers

Slipped (or skipped) stitch patterns are created by slipping or skipping individual needles. The slipped needles do not form stitches and the working yarn strand is carried UNDER the needles (as opposed to Tuck, where the working yarn is carried OVER the needles)
Machine knitting charts will often use these symbols to indicate SLIP

Punchcards
Because multiple needles can be slipped, a variety of punchcards can be used.
As an LK-150 knitter, you will need to "translate" the black and white holes in punchards for your machine. We will cover this in a following lesson.
HINT
For Slip, needles in "B" (working position) DO NOT Knit. Needles in "C" or "D" knit. (this differs from tuck). So the logic for hand selecting needles is different for slip than tuck.
Because the strands are carried across the purl side of the work, the obvious choice for the "right side" (public side) of the knitting is the purl side. But this versatile stitch has more uses!

Slip stitch has a variety of uses

in addition to adding texture to your knitting and color work with NO FLOATS.

Free Pass

Your working yarn is on one side of the knitting and your carriage is on the other. Maybe you've ripped out some rows or just need to move the carriage across the knitting WITHOUT dropping stitches.

Check out the "Free Pass Refresher" lesson in this course.
Also watch the "Single Row Stripes" lesson below.

Single Row Stripes

Add color interest to your knitting with single row stripes using Slip Free Pass

Marker Row

Here are 3 methods of creating a marker row - including slip stitch

Slip Cord (I-Cord)

I-cord (or slip cord) can be used in many ways to embellish your knitting. It can be used as shoulder straps for girls dresses, belts and decorative ties … the list is endless! Machine knitters can quickly make I-cord and it is an essential technique for beginners to learn.
This technique can also be used for decorative finishing edge for your knitting.

Slip Cast on

Here's a fast, closed cast on that can be worked on any machine. Use the slip setting, your cast on comb and get knitting FAST!

The previous exercises were designed to help you UNDERSTAND the concepts of the Slip settings on your machine.

components.html:
Plating (also called plaiting or platting) is the process where 2 different yarns are knitted together. It is more than running 2 ends together, the machine separates the strands so one strand appears on the knit side and the other strand appears on the purl side of the knitting.

Why use Plating?

  1. Knit reversible fabric with 2 different kind of yarn. Consider using different colors and/or textures.
  2. Give body to thin, wimpy yarn. Combine the thin yarn or plait it with a more substantial yarn.
  3. Reinforce heels, knees, elbows
  4. Create unusual fabrics mixing plating with tuck

components.html:
Plating is controlled by the feeder carriage. It positions the working yarn to create the technique.

Consider the yarn weight:


When plating, 2 strands are being knit together. Choose 2 yarns that COMBINED total a weight appropriate for your machine. Remember that the 2 yarns together need to fit in the hooks of the needles.
We choosing yarn, also consider the finished weight of the garment.

Knit at a looser tension


Because you are "bulking-up" the yarn plan to set your tension dial 1-2 numbers looser.
Mix 'n Match
Consider:
  • Combine a thicker yarn with a thin yarn
  • 2 fine yarns together
  • A textured yarn with a plain yarn
  • A variegated yarn with a plain color yarn

Swatch the same way you would for any other stitch pattern ... you do swatch... don't you???

components.title: Threading the carriage for plating can be a bit tricky.

components.html:
To better understand plating and to get inspired to use this technique, try the following exercise with different yarns.

Set your tension dial to a looser tension (how loose? It depends on the yarn you've chosen)
Using 2 strands of yarn,(not too heavy! - 1/2 the weight you'd usually use with your machine)
Cast on 30 stitches. Use any method you'd like, but add even weight. With BOTH STRANDS in the #1 (main) yarn feeder, knit a few inches.
  • Is it hard to knit? - USE a thinner yarn
  • As you knit, feel the resulting knitting and judge the tension - adjust as you like.
Re-thread the carriage - putting one yarn in each slot
  • Knit a few inches
  • Note which color yarn is facing you as you knit (the purl side of the knitting)
Reverse the yarns in the feeders
  • Knit a few inches
  • Note which color yarn is facing you as you knit (the purl side of the knitting)

Repeat this exercise with different yarns in both color, weight and texture. Get Creative!

components.html:
Fairisle (or stranded) knitting can be worked on your LK-150 machine.
Although this is a manual machine (no punchcards or electronics), knitting simple fairisle patterns is still A LOT quicker than knitting by hand.
In addition, with practice, your knitting will be a lot more even and stitches more uniform that knitting by hand.
The key to successful Fairisle knitting on this machine is not so much learning the levers, but being able to read and follow charts to hand select needles.
If you've followed this course from the beginning, you should already know how to set the machine for Fairisle!

If you skipped the section on Slip Stitch - go back and work through all the exercises!

components.html:
Duplicate the exercise demonstrated in the video in the previous lesson. 2 rows of 3 stitch dashes.
Try this practice more than once with different needle combinations until you get comfortable with reading your knitting and following a chart.

Choose 2 contrasting colors of yarn of similar weight. Name them Color A and Color B
Get started
  1. With Color A, cast on 33 stitches (multiple of 6 plus 3)
  2. Use any cast on method of your choice
  3. Knit for 2", end with the carriage on the right

If you aren't familiar with stitch multiples check the tutorial in the "Miscellaneous" section below

1. Engage the SIDE LEVERS
  2. Starting at the right edge, pull groups of 3 needles to "D" position
  3. Remove color A from the carriage and secure it in the yarn rest
  4. Thread the carriage with color B
  5. Knit from right to left

Be sure both end needles are in "D" position

1. Starting at the right edge, pull THE SAME GROUPS of 3 needles to "D" position
  2. With Color B still threaded, knit from LEFT to RIGHT

Before knitting the row, confirm the Side Levers are engaged and the Russel Levers are dis-engaged

1. Pull the OPPOSITE groups of 3 needles to "D" position
  2. Change to color A and knit from RIGHT to LEFT

Note that the color B stitches are not knitting

1. Pull the THE SAME groups of 3 needles to "D" position
  2. With Color A still threaded knit from LEFT to RIGHT

When changing colors and both working yarns are on the same side, release both of them and allow the take up spring to untangle. Be sure to "Milk the Cow" to prevent sloppy edges.

1. Break color B and weave the tails over the needles in work
  2. Change to color A and knit a few inches
  3. Bind off or drop the work from the machine

Stretch the knitting both ways to "pop" the stitches in place this will create uniform stitches.

components.html:
Perfect Joins

When working intarsia, the challenge is keeping the edges of the adjoining colors uniform and neat.
Here are 3 methods for you to try:
  1. Twist the working yarns
    Just like in hand knitting, Any time 2 working yarns are next to each other, twist the yarns to prevent a hole.
  2. Wrap the working yarns
    Similar to wrapping when working short rows, wrap the working yarn around the held needle next to it. You can see this demonstrated in the video in the section "What is Intarsia? The Mechanics"
  3. Carry a separate "binding" yarn up the join
    Before you start knitting, reserve a strand of the main color yarn. At the join of 2 colors, lay the binding yarn across the end needles of the adjoining sections. Zig Zag this yarn back and forth "binding" the edges as you knit. Some knitters will e-wrap this binding yarn. Others will use a binding yarn IN ADDITION to another method.
